newsitem.title: CHINA: China crackdown wounds unhealed as HK return looms.
newsitem.headline: China crackdown wounds unhealed as HK return looms.

text.p: China's state propaganda machine may be focused firmly on the imminent return of Hong Kong to Beijing rule, but the minds of many in the Chinese capital are on a different date in the nation's political calender.

The eighth anniversary of the crushing of pro-democracy protests in Beijing has prompted private and public calls for an official re-evaluation of the events of June 4, 1989, from dissidents, relatives of those killed and ordinary residents.

"Even animals will resist if you kill their children," said Zhou Shuzhuang, whose 24-year-old son was shot dead by soldiers as they forced their way into the heart of Beijing to halt the student-led protests in central Tiananmen Square in 1989.

The families of the dead could not forget their loved ones and would continue to press for a reversal of the official verdict on the crackdown despite the state's efforts to force them into silence, said Zhou, 61, in a recent interview.

"They want us to die, so we won't speak out. So we have to go on living," said the retired official, one of 42 bereaved relatives who this month signed a petition calling on China's parliament to hold an official inquiry into the killings.

No hint of such calls have made it into the pages of China's state-controlled newspapers, which have for weeks been pumping out a steady flow of triumphant reports on the July 1 return to China of the British colony of Hong Kong.
The June 4 crackdown has cast a shadow over the handover in Hong Kong, where protests against Beijing's use of force against unarmed students have been an annual fixture since 1989.
China has stuck to its line that tough action was needed to end a counter-revolutionary rebellion sparked by student protests.

While police and security forces step up their vigilance for the period around June 4, keeping close watch on dissidents and victims' families, little official notice is taken of the most sensitive day in the Chinese political diary.

An article defending Beijing's human rights record in the official China Daily made no direct mention of the crackdown, although the newspaper warned Western nations not to focus on "single events or persons".

Sensitivities around this year's anniversary have been raised by the death in February of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who put the final seal of approval on the use of soldiers and tanks to crush the pro-democracy protests.

Analysts say Deng's death at 92 could give his political heirs more freedom of action on the thorny legacy of the Tiananmen movement and could even prompt official condemnation of the use of force and rehabilitation of the victims.
"While Deng Xiaoping was alive, this case could not be overturned," said dissident Jiang Qisheng, who was jailed for his role as a student organiser of the 1989 democracy movement.
"I'm very confident, it will (now) certainly be overturned," he said, but added it was unclear how long it would take the Communist Party to alter its stance.
Many Chinese still yearn for an accounting over the 1989 crackdown, with debate over the government's handling of the protests spilling onto the Internet worldwide computer network.
Many contributors to recent on-line discussions have expressed anger at the government's use of force, but some also have criticised the Tiananmen Square demonstrators for pushing the state too far.
The government had mishandled the affair, but protesters should have gone home after martial law was declared, said one Internet user, who gave his identity only as 'A Student'.
"Through the blood of June 4, the Chinese people have had a deep lesson in the law," he said. "Never again will large numbers of residents disobey martial law."
